payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
Every design for signing music at creation eventually reaches the same sentence: the artist holds the key. Earlier notes here ended on it, once as the choice between a distributor holding the stamp for the artist and the artist holding it, and once as the variable nobody has tested yet. The sentence is right. It also skips the part a working musician would ask about first, which is where that key physically sits on an ordinary Tuesday.

One key is the wrong number

A single key on a single laptop fails the day the laptop does. Everything it signed stays verifiable, but nothing new can be signed under that name, the same freeze that a lost key causes for a living artist as much as for an estate. Copying the key onto every machine fixes that and opens a worse hole, because one stolen phone can now sign anything and date it to any year. Syncing it through a cloud account sounds like the middle path. It puts the account provider's recovery desk inside the chain of identity, which is the institution the whole model was built to step around.

Web security settled this long ago. The key at the top of a certificate chain stays offline, and its only job is to vouch for the keys beneath it. Those lower keys do the daily work and can be replaced without touching the top.

A drawer and a chip

Applied to a musician, the top key lives on a security key, a small device of the kind many people already use to log in. It sits in a drawer and comes out when a new computer joins the setup or an old one leaves, and for nothing else. Some of these devices have their own screen, so the musician reads what is being approved on the device itself, where a compromised laptop cannot rewrite it.

Daily signing happens elsewhere. Most laptops and phones sold in recent years carry a chip that handles face and fingerprint unlock, and that chip can generate a key no software can copy out. Each machine gets its own. The drawer key signs one short statement per machine: this key may sign for me until this date. Whether the musician signs at export or at upload, the signature comes from a machine they own.

What a verifier checks, starting from the track

The track. Its signature checks against the key of the machine that made it.

The machine. Its key appears in a statement saying it may sign for this person until a given date.

The drawer. That statement carries the drawer key's signature, the one key the whole chain rests on.

Each link is checked on its own, so the links do not even need the same kind of signature math, which matters because the chips in phones and the devices in drawers can use different ones. The chain also records which machine signed, so a vocal tracked on the studio desktop and a melody sketched on a phone can carry different names if the artist wants that shown.

When a machine goes missing

A stolen laptop becomes an errand. The drawer key withdraws that machine's permission and nothing else changes. Records the laptop signed before the theft face the same fork every revocation does, and anchoring each record when it is made is what turns the theft date into a clean line. Permissions that lapse on their own, a year at a time, cover the machine nobody remembered to withdraw. What lapses is the permission to sign new work. A record anchored while that permission was live keeps standing, since expiring it would destroy the record it exists to protect.

Losing the drawer key is rarer and worse. A recovery phrase written on paper when the device was set up restores it. Lose both and the musician is back at the freeze, where every way out involves someone else holding a copy.

None of this is new engineering, and software publishers have run versions of it for years. What the chain cannot do is say whose drawer it is. Every link checks all the way up to a key that belongs to someone, and tying that top key to a name is a separate problem the drawer leaves exactly where it found it.

References

Apple. "Protecting keys with the Secure Enclave." Apple Developer Documentation. Accessed October 2026. developer.apple.com

Microsoft. "Trusted Platform Module Technology Overview." Microsoft Learn. Accessed October 2026. learn.microsoft.com

Cooper, D., Santesson, S., Farrell, S., Boeyen, S., Housley, R., and Polk, W. "Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and Certificate Revocation List (CRL) Profile." RFC 5280, May 2008. rfc-editor.org

W3C. "Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0." W3C Recommendation, May 15, 2025. w3.org
